takeaway: cleAR learns a failed atomic region’s cache-line footprint, then locks suitable footprints on retry so many transactions avoid repeated speculation and coarse-grained fallback.
background: Hardware transactional memory and speculative lock elision run atomic regions concurrently, detect conflicts, and roll back failed work. Implementations eventually serialize repeatedly failing regions with a fallback lock.
villain: Contention can cause repeated aborts and expensive coarse-grained fallback, yet software usually does not know the region’s complete address footprint early enough to lock only the needed cache lines.
approach: During an initial speculative execution, cleAR tracks accessed cache lines and propagates dependency bits to judge whether the footprint can change; after a conflict, discovery continues to the region’s end when hardware resources permit. A small immutable, lockable footprint retries non-speculatively after locking all lines in a deadlock-free order, while a possibly mutable footprint locks selected lines but retains speculative rollback. Larger or unconvertible regions use the ordinary speculative retry or fallback path, with no source-program changes.
impact: The authors argue that dynamically combining speculation with fine-grained cache-line locking can preserve low-contention concurrency while bounding retries for the eligible subset of atomic regions.

evaluation.overview: The authors use full-system gem5 to measure execution time, aborts, commit modes, fallback frequency, and McPAT-modeled energy on data-structure programs, two standalone applications, and the STAMP suite.
evaluation.implemented: A simulated TSX-like HTM core extended with register dependency bits, per-region discovery state, a 32-entry Address to Lock Table, a Conflicting Reads Table, cache-line locking and coherence changes, totaling less than 1 KiB per core.
evaluation.setting: The model is a 32-core Ice-Lake-like out-of-order x86 system running Ubuntu 18.04 and Linux 5.4.49; applications use 32 threads. Each configuration runs ten seeds, discards three outliers for a trimmed mean, and selects the best-performing retry limit for each application from one through ten.

results.text: Across the simulated benchmark set, the authors report that cleAR over PowerTM reduced average execution time by 35.0% versus requester-wins HTM and by 23.3% versus PowerTM.
The baseline completed 35.4% of retried regions on the first retry and sent 37.2% to fallback; cleAR over PowerTM changed those shares to 64.4% and 15.4%, respectively.
results.locator: §7, “Bounding ARs to a Single Retry,” Figure 13

limitations: The single-retry guarantee applies only when discovery finishes and the learned footprint is small, simultaneously lockable, and immutable; mutable or large regions can still retry or fall back, and many STAMP regions exceed the modeled discovery resources. All results are simulation-based and use a per-application retry limit selected by design-space exploration.
phd_group_signal: The work reflects a concurrency-architecture style that derives correctness conditions first, adds explicit microarchitectural state and coherence behavior, and then studies both common-case speed and fallback behavior in full-system simulation.

claims.text: cleAR extends speculative execution with a discovery phase that learns cache-line addresses and footprint mutability, then chooses non-speculative cache-line locking, speculative cache-line locking, an ordinary retry, or fallback according to the learned conditions.

Completion on a single retry is guaranteed only for regions whose complete footprint fits discovery resources, remains immutable, and can be locked simultaneously in the prescribed order; the speculative locking mode does not provide that unconditional guarantee.
